topic: PD micrographia: prevalence and clinical correlates
citation: Wagle Shukla A, Ounpraseuth S, Okun MS, Gray V, Schwankhaus J, Metzer WS. Micrographia and related deficits in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open 2012;2(3):e000628.
task_or_setup: Micrographia asked on history, plus a handwriting test: lowercase print 'p' and 'd' written 20 times in two rows (4 blocks of 5); micrographia = area of last block >=30% smaller than first block (severe = >50%). Bradykinesia by finger tap, Purdue pegboard and timed walk; hypophonia by decibel meter. Tested in the usual ON medication state.
participants_or_bench: 68 PD (all men; Veterans Administration movement-disorders clinic; mean age 72.3 +/- 9.5 y; disease duration 7.8 +/- 5.5 y). Excluded: severe tremor, dystonia, dyskinesia, stroke, neuropathy, dementia. Controls used only to validate test scores.
comparator: Self-report vs handwriting test; controls for test validation
key_quantitative_findings: Micrographia on history 63.2% (43/68); on handwriting test ~50% (35/68); severe (>50% area drop) n=12. Test vs history: sensitivity 0.74 (95% CI 0.59-0.86), specificity 0.88 (0.68-0.97). Test-defined micrographia correlated with age (p=0.02), MMSE (p=0.04), hypophonia by history (p=0.01) and quantitative bradykinesia (Purdue pegboard, p=0.04). No correlation with L-DOPA equivalent dose.
units_and_conditions: Area ratio (%) of last vs first block of letters; ON medication; no letter heights in mm reported.
locator: Abstract; Methods (handwriting test, Figure 1); Results (correlates); Discussion (limitations)
limitations: Cross-sectional, single visit; all-male veteran cohort; unblinded raters; ON state only, so medication effect not tested; >=30% area criterion is study-specific; severe-tremor patients excluded.
relevance_to_design: About half of clinic PD patients show a measurable within-task size decrement; the deficit is a size-scaling problem across a sequence of letters, not sub-millimetre positional noise.
transferability_reason: Clinic cohort of older male veterans; prevalence depends on the task and threshold used.
design_implication: A +/-0.5 mm local nib offset cannot restore a 30-50% loss of letter-block area accumulated along a line. Target micrographia with size-feedback and cueing modes. Do not use the pen to detect micrographia.
search_query: WebSearch: Wagle Shukla 2012 BMJ Open micrographia and related deficits in Parkinson's disease cross-sectional study; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3383984/

topic: PD micrographia: historical prevalence (secondary)
citation: McLennan JE, Nakano K, Tyler HR, Schwab RS. Micrographia in Parkinson's disease. J Neurol Sci 1972;15(2):141-152.
task_or_setup: Per Thomas et al. 2017: handwriting samples collected from selected patients who had significant, observable micrographia. Original methods not verified.
participants_or_bench: Not verified. The abstract is withheld by the publisher (Semantic Scholar/Crossref) and ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403.
key_quantitative_findings: Secondary accounts only. Thomas et al. 2017: McLennan et al. reported that micrographia 'may be observed in approximately 5% of patients with PD before the onset of motor symptoms, and 30% of those patients later report further worsening of handwriting', and remarked that the 'nature of data did not lend itself readily to quantification'. Eklund et al. 2022 cite McLennan 1972 for levodopa increasing handwriting size in consistent micrographia. A web-search summary attributed '10-15%' severe micrographia to McLennan; no retrieved text confirms this.
units_and_conditions: Visual/qualitative. No mm or % size data verified.
locator: Thomas 2017 (PMC6174397), section 'Handwriting Analysis: Journey from Paper-and-Pen to Digitizing Tablets'; Eklund 2022, Introduction
limitations: Original not accessed; selected sample; non-quantitative; secondary accounts may be imprecise and are partly inconsistent.
relevance_to_design: Historical anchor only.
transferability_reason: Unverified figures; visual assessment; cohort characteristics unknown.
design_implication: Do not put McLennan-derived percentages into requirements. Use the quantified cohorts (PDT-01, PDT-04, PDT-05, PDT-06).
search_query: WebSearch: McLennan 1972 micrographia Parkinson's disease "95 patients" OR "15%" OR "5%" prevalence Schwab; Europe PMC: AUTH:"McLennan JE" AND TITLE:micrographia; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6174397/

topic: PD handwriting impairment overview (micrographia, dysgraphia, medication response)
citation: Thomas M, Lenka A, Kumar Pal P. Handwriting Analysis in Parkinson's Disease: Current Status and Future Directions. Mov Disord Clin Pract 2017;4(6):806-818.
task_or_setup: Narrative review of PubMed/SCOPUS literature on kinematic handwriting analysis in PD.
participants_or_bench: n/a (review)
key_quantitative_findings: Definitions: consistent micrographia = 'an overall reduction in letter size compared with that before the onset of PD'; progressive = 'decreasing letter size as writing progresses'. 'The exact prevalence of micrographia in PD is not clear and may range from 9% to 60%'. 'Letter size improves in only 50% of patients in response to medications', whereas velocity, fluency and acceleration measures are more medication-sensitive (Poluha 1998, Tucha 2006, Lange 2006, Table 1). Bajaj et al.: micrographia more prevalent in akinetic-rigid than tremor-dominant PD (90% sensitivity, 55% specificity for the akinetic-rigid phenotype). Rosenblum 2013: PD applied less pen pressure than controls. Fluency measures: NIV/NIA, jerk, ratio of deceleration phase.
units_and_conditions: Percentages (prevalence); qualitative kinematic findings.
locator: Sections 'Spectrum of Handwriting Abnormalities in PD - Micrographia', 'The Concept of PD Dysgraphia', 'Newly Proposed Additional Parameters'; Table 1; Figure 4
limitations: Narrative, non-systematic review; heterogeneous definitions; secondary account of the cited primary studies.
relevance_to_design: PD writing impairment involves size, speed, fluency and pressure. Tremor-dominant PD has less micrographia.
transferability_reason: Review synthesis of heterogeneous tablet studies.
design_implication: Design PD modes around size and fluency, not tremor. Tremor correction matters, if at all, only for the tremor-dominant subgroup. Outcome sets should cover size, velocity, fluency (NIV or jerk) and pressure.
search_query: WebSearch: Thomas Lenka Pal 2017 handwriting analysis in Parkinson's disease current status and future directions micrographia prevalence; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6174397/

topic: PD micrographia: prevalence depends on task
citation: Kim EJ, Lee BH, Park KC, Lee WY, Na DL. Micrographia on free writing versus copying tasks in idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Parkinsonism Relat Disord 2005;11(1):57-63.
task_or_setup: Free writing vs copying of a target letter or figure. Consistent micrographia (CM) = mean size below controls' mean-2SD; progressive micrographia (PM) = slope of size vs serial position below controls' mean-2SD.
participants_or_bench: 75 idiopathic PD; 30 sex/age-matched healthy controls
comparator: Healthy controls; free writing vs copying
key_quantitative_findings: Free writing: 1/75 met CM and 2/75 met PM. Letter/figure copying: 33/75 (44%) CM and 19/75 (25%) PM.
units_and_conditions: Counts/% of patients; size units not given in abstract; medication state not stated in abstract.
locator: Abstract (Results)
limitations: Abstract only; single centre; Korean script; the -2SD criterion depends on the control sample.
relevance_to_design: Measured micrographia ranges from about 1% to 44% depending on whether writing is free or copied to a target.
transferability_reason: Task- and script-specific, but the effect of method is large.
design_implication: Guided-practice modes should use target-referenced copying to reveal and train size. Any size metric needs a controlled task.
search_query: Europe PMC REST: TITLE:"Micrographia on free writing versus copying tasks"

topic: PD progressive micrographia: magnitude in mm
citation: Zham P, Raghav S, Kempster P, Poosapadi Arjunan S, Wong K, Nagao KJ, Kumar DK. A Kinematic Study of Progressive Micrographia in Parkinson's Disease. Front Neurol 2019;10:403.
task_or_setup: Repeated cursive letter 'e' (>20 repetitions) on a Wacom Intuos Pro-Large capturing x-y and pen pressure at 133 Hz. Progressive micrographia (PMG) = >10% decrement in letter stroke length (mean of first vs last five letters).
participants_or_bench: 24 PD (disease duration <10 y, mean 5 +/- 2.88 y) in practically defined OFF state (medication withheld >=12 h); 24 age-matched controls
key_quantitative_findings: 66% of PD (16/24) showed PMG. In the PMG group, median stroke length fell from 18.97 mm (initial) to 14.61 mm (final), effect size r=0.62; controls 19.4 to 19.44 mm. No significant change in speed or acceleration across the task in the PMG group, and no correlation with overall OFF-state motor disability. Only one patient showed a purely consistent pattern.
units_and_conditions: Stroke length in mm; OFF medication; letter 'e' repeated task.
locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods (participants; experimental methods); Table 4; Discussion
limitations: Small sample; OFF state only (no levodopa comparison); single repeated-letter task; stroke-length definition specific to this study.
relevance_to_design: Size decrement in PD is millimetres over about 20 letters (~4.4 mm stroke-length loss), far beyond +/-0.5 mm.
transferability_reason: OFF-state lab task likely exaggerates everyday deficit; small n.
design_implication: Progressive size loss needs sequence-level feedback (e.g., cue or alert when stroke length falls >10% from the start), not local nib displacement.
search_query: WebSearch: Letanneux 2014 "From micrographia to Parkinson's disease dysgraphia" consistent progressive micrographia prevalence; WebFetch: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2019.00403/full

topic: PD vs ET vs controls: letter size in mm; ET has no micrographia
citation: Eklund M, Nuuttila S, Joutsa J, Jaakkola E, Mäkinen E, Honkanen EA, Lindholm K, Vahlberg T, Noponen T, Ihalainen T, Murtomäki K, Nojonen T, Levo R, Mertsalmi T, Scheperjans F, Kaasinen V. Diagnostic value of micrographia in Parkinson's disease: a study with [123I]FP-CIT SPECT. J Neural Transm 2022;129:895-904.
task_or_setup: Pen on blank paper: draw a house and write one Finnish sentence ('Today is a beautiful day'). Heights of 'T', 'p', 'a' measured with a ruler; writing area = mean height x width. Progressive micrographia = slope (b) of heights of letters 'a'. Criteria: below -2 SD of healthy controls. DAT-SPECT in all participants.
participants_or_bench: 146 PD (28 on levodopa; many early/unmedicated), 42 ET, 38 healthy controls (age 50-85)
key_quantitative_findings: Median (IQR) letter height: PD 4.3 (1.9) mm, ET 5.0 (1.7) mm, HC 5.0 (1.4) mm. Writing area: PD 399 (301), ET 536 (397), HC 548 (286) mm^2. PD letters 14.0% smaller than ET and HC; area 25.6% smaller than ET and 27.2% smaller than HC. No ET-HC difference (p=1.0). Progressive slope b: PD -0.14, ET -0.06, HC -0.06. By -2SD criteria, 13/146 PD had consistent and 13/146 progressive micrographia (none both). No difference between levodopa-medicated and unmedicated PD (p>0.24). Letter height correlated with MDS-UPDRS motor (r=-0.21) and bradykinesia (r=-0.21). No correlation with DAT binding.
units_and_conditions: mm and mm^2 (ruler); one-sentence free writing; mixed medication states.
locator: Abstract; Methods 'Evaluation of micrographia'; Table 1; Results 'Group differences' and 'Group differences between patients with and without micrographia'
limitations: Single short sentence; ruler measurement; language-specific cut-offs; mostly early PD; free writing is less sensitive than copying (see PDT-04).
relevance_to_design: Early PD average letter-height deficit is ~0.7 mm (4.3 vs 5.0 mm) and cumulative across a line. ET writing size is normal.
transferability_reason: Large, well-characterised cohort, but Finnish and a single sentence.
design_implication: ET users need tremor handling, not size cueing. PD users need size cueing. The pen must not claim to tell PD from ET: 56.8% sensitivity / 78.6% specificity even in this study.
search_query: WebSearch: Letanneux 2014 "From micrographia to Parkinson's disease dysgraphia" consistent progressive micrographia prevalence; WebFetch: https://d-nb.info/1265368090/34 (PDF text extracted locally)

topic: Tremor definitions and frequency bands (rest, action, kinetic, re-emergent, writing, physiological)
citation: Bhatia KP, Bain P, Bajaj N, Elble RJ, Hallett M, Louis ED, Raethjen J, Stamelou M, Testa CM, Deuschl G; Tremor Task Force of the International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society. Consensus Statement on the classification of tremors. Mov Disord 2018;33(1):75-87.
task_or_setup: International consensus classification (literature search plus consensus meetings).
participants_or_bench: n/a (expert consensus)
key_quantitative_findings: Rest tremor: tremor in a body part not voluntarily activated. Action tremor: postural or kinetic. Task-specific tremor occurs during tasks such as writing; primary writing tremor occurs only when writing. ET: isolated bilateral upper-limb action tremor for >=3 years without parkinsonism, dystonia or ataxia. In PD the 'amplitude of rest tremor almost always diminishes or is abolished, at least transiently, during goal-directed voluntary movements'. Re-emergent tremor: delayed re-emergence when a new posture is held. Frequencies: physiological 8-12 Hz; most pathological tremors 4-8 Hz; primary orthostatic 13-18 Hz. Physiological tremor is 'generally not visible or symptomatic unless it is enhanced by fatigue or anxiety'.
units_and_conditions: Frequency in Hz; definitional.
locator: Sections on activation condition, ET criteria, task-specific tremor and physiological tremor
limitations: Definitions, not measurements. No displacement amplitudes.
relevance_to_design: PD rest tremor is expected to shrink during writing, but re-emergent tremor can appear while the pen is held still. Pathological tremor (4-8 Hz) sits above most voluntary movement content (<2 Hz per Elble & McNames 2016, screened), but the margin during fast handwriting strokes has not been measured.
transferability_reason: Field-standard definitions.
design_implication: Tremor handling must work in the 4-12 Hz band and must not depend on a diagnosis label. Expect PD tremor mainly during pauses and hovering, not during strokes.
search_query: Europe PMC REST: TITLE:"Consensus Statement on the classification of tremors"; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6530552/

topic: PD: prevalence of rest, postural, kinetic and action tremor
citation: Gupta DK, Marano M, Zweber C, Boyd JT, Kuo SH. Prevalence and Relationship of Rest Tremor and Action Tremor in Parkinson's Disease. Tremor Other Hyperkinet Mov 2020;10:58.
task_or_setup: Secondary analysis of MDS-UPDRS part III items 3.15 (postural), 3.16 (kinetic, finger-to-nose) and 3.17 (rest amplitude) at baseline; each tremor type present if score >=1; action tremor requires both postural and kinetic tremor.
participants_or_bench: PPMI n=423 (early, drug-naive); BioFIND n=118 (moderate-advanced, treated); PDBP n=873 (mixed; 90.8% treated)
comparator: Between cohorts; with vs without rest tremor
key_quantitative_findings: Rest tremor 68.6% / 63.6% / 52.0%; postural 52.7% / 58.5% / 46.7%; kinetic 51.3% / 51.7% / 52.5%; action tremor 36.9% / 39.0% / 35.8% (PPMI / BioFIND / PDBP). Action tremor more prevalent with rest tremor (PDBP 49.9% vs 21.0%).
units_and_conditions: % of patients with item score >=1; clinical ratings, no displacement data; writing not assessed.
locator: Table 3; Results
limitations: Score >=1 includes 'slight' tremor; kinetic tremor rated on finger-to-nose, not writing; no amplitude in mm; mixed medication states.
relevance_to_design: About half of PD patients have some kinetic tremor, mostly slight; amplitude during writing is unknown.
transferability_reason: Large cohorts but clinical items, not writing; slight tremor is not quantified.
design_implication: Tremor correction could matter for a subset of PD users. Measure PD writing tremor directly before sizing the actuator for PD.
search_query: WebSearch: action tremor Parkinson's disease prevalence kinetic postural re-emergent tremor frequency Hz cohort study; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7757606/

topic: PD: re-emergent tremor (latency, frequency)
citation: Jankovic J, Schwartz KS, Ondo W. Re-emergent tremor of Parkinson's disease. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1999;67(5):646-650.
task_or_setup: Latency and frequency of postural tremor measured after assuming an outstretched posture.
participants_or_bench: 18 PD with postural tremor (mean age 63.2 y); 20 ET (66.9 y); 7 ET+PD (68.7 y)
key_quantitative_findings: Re-emergent tremor present in 12/18 PD; latency 9.37 (SD 10.66) s, significantly longer than ET postural tremor latency (p<0.0005). Mean frequency ~5.5 Hz, no different from typical PD rest tremor. PD postural tremor amplitudes generally higher than ET.
units_and_conditions: Seconds; Hz; posture task, not writing.
locator: Abstract (PMC1736624)
limitations: Abstract only; selected sample of PD patients with postural tremor; no writing task; amplitude units not in abstract.
relevance_to_design: In PD, tremor may appear after seconds of steady pen holding (pauses, hovering, dot-holding) at rest-tremor frequency.
transferability_reason: Posture task; selected patients.
design_implication: Log tremor during pen-down pauses and hover separately from strokes, and allow a latency of several seconds before tremor onset.
search_query: WebSearch: Jankovic re-emergent tremor Parkinson's disease latency frequency prevalence 1999 JNNP; WebFetch: https://scholars.houstonmethodist.org/en/publications/re-emergent-tremor-of-parkinsons-disease/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1736624/

topic: PD: tremor detected during handwriting (tablet)
citation: Smits EJ, Tolonen AJ, Cluitmans L, van Gils M, Conway BA, Zietsma RC, Leenders KL, Maurits NM. Standardized handwriting to assess bradykinesia, micrographia and tremor in Parkinson's disease. PLoS One 2014;9(5):e97614.
task_or_setup: 'elelelel' x10, a Dutch sentence x10, plus circle, spiral and star tracing on a Wacom Intuos 2 at 100 Hz (MovAlyzeR). Tremor = spectral peak (Welch) of the first principal component of acceleration.
participants_or_bench: 10 PD (modified H&Y 1-2.5; median duration 4.4 y) after overnight medication withdrawal; severe hand tremor (UPDRS-III >=3) excluded; 10 age-matched controls
key_quantitative_findings: Peak PSD >30 (mm/s^2)/Hz in the 3 PD patients clinically rated as having rest tremor, vs <2 (mm/s^2)/Hz in all other participants. Their peak frequencies were 8.0, 5.3 and 4.4 Hz. Width of 'e' significantly smaller in PD (p<0.0014); time per repetition, velocity and acceleration differed (p<0.0014).
units_and_conditions: Acceleration PSD ((mm/s^2)/Hz) and Hz; OFF medication; displacement amplitude not reported.
locator: Methods (inclusion, tremor analysis); Results (tremor, micrographia, bradykinesia)
limitations: n=10; severe tremor excluded; acceleration spectra only (no mm); no comparison with clinical exam.
relevance_to_design: Writing tremor was detectable in 3/10 mildly affected OFF-state PD patients, all with rest tremor, at 4.4-8 Hz.
transferability_reason: Very small sample; excluded severe tremor; OFF state.
design_implication: Writing tremor probably affects a minority of PD users. PD writing-tremor displacement in mm is still unmeasured and is a gap.
search_query: WebSearch: "handwriting" tremor Parkinson's disease tablet spectral analysis tremor frequency amplitude during writing mm; WebFetch: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0097614

topic: Tremor rating vs measured amplitude (log relation), incl. writing and spirals
citation: Elble RJ, Pullman SL, Matsumoto JY, Raethjen J, Deuschl G, Tintner R; Tremor Research Group. Tremor amplitude is logarithmically related to 4- and 5-point tremor rating scales. Brain 2006;129(10):2660-2666.
task_or_setup: Pooled data from five laboratories: graphics tablet (3 labs), accelerometer (3 labs), mechanical linkage (1 lab); writing, drawing, posture, rest, finger-nose tasks graded with various 0-4 scales.
participants_or_bench: 928 patients with various hand tremors
key_quantitative_findings: log relation in all labs: T2/T1 = 10^(alpha x (TRS2-TRS1)), T in cm. alpha = 0.414-0.441 for writing; 0.355-0.574 for spiral drawing; 0.441-0.488 rest; 0.266-0.577 postural; 0.306 finger-nose. A 1-point TRS decrease = amplitude ratio 0.501/0.398/0.316/0.251/0.200 for alpha 0.3/0.4/0.5/0.6/0.7. For writing (alpha ~0.43) one rating point = ~2.6-2.8x amplitude (derived from abstract values).
units_and_conditions: cm (displacement); intercepts and amplitude convention (peak vs peak-to-peak) not available in abstract.
locator: Abstract (full text paywalled)
limitations: Abstract only: no intercepts, so ratings cannot be converted to absolute mm from this source; pooled diagnoses and devices.
relevance_to_design: A clinically visible 1-point writing-tremor change is a ~2.7x amplitude change. Small absolute corrections move ratings very little when tremor is large.
transferability_reason: Relation replicated across 5 labs and devices.
design_implication: Express nib-correction benefit as % amplitude reduction and translate it to expected rating change. Obtain intercepts for handwriting (see PDT-12 for spirals).
search_query: WebSearch: Elble 2006 Brain tremor amplitude is logarithmically related to 4- and 5-point tremor rating scales; Europe PMC REST: EXT_ID:16891320 AND SRC:MED

topic: ET spiral tremor amplitude distribution (tablet, peak-to-peak) and rating-amplitude intercept
citation: Elble RJ, Ellenbogen A. Digitizing Tablet and Fahn-Tolosa-Marín Ratings of Archimedes Spirals have Comparable Minimum Detectable Change in Essential Tremor. Tremor Other Hyperkinet Mov 2017;7:481.
task_or_setup: Large and small FTM Archimedes spirals, each hand, on paper mounted on a Wacom Intuos 3 (100 samples/s; accuracy +/-0.25 mm). Tremor from spectral analysis by a blinded central lab. Per-patient grand average of mean peak-to-peak displacement over the 4 spirals. Two baselines on consecutive days.
participants_or_bench: 18 ET (14 M, 4 F; 60 +/- 8.7 y), mild to severe; off tremor drugs >=5 half-lives; no alcohol or caffeine for 48 h (sodium oxybate PK/PD trial NCT00598078)
key_quantitative_findings: Tablet amplitude geometric mean 0.20 cm (baseline 1) and 0.19 cm (baseline 2) peak-to-peak; arithmetic mean 0.62 cm (baseline 1). Data positively skewed; log10 values approx. normal (D'Agostino-Pearson p=0.25). Mean FTM spiral rating 0.88 and 0.94 (floor effect at 0). log10 T(cm) = 0.6 x FTM - 1.27 (r=0.94; text uses -1.26). Implied (derived) p-p amplitude: FTM 0 = 0.54 mm, 0.5 = 1.07 mm, 1 = 2.14 mm, 1.5 = 4.3 mm, 2 = 8.5 mm. Test-retest ICC: tablet 0.97, FTM 0.90. MDC: tablet 51% of baseline geometric mean; FTM 67% (amplitude-equivalent). Lognormal fit (derived from GM and AM; sigma_log10 ~0.65): ~8% <=0.25 mm, ~18% <=0.5 mm, ~32% <=1 mm, ~50% <=2 mm, ~68% <=4 mm peak-to-peak.
units_and_conditions: cm peak-to-peak displacement from tablet spectra; spirals, not handwriting; averaged across both hands and two spiral sizes; drug-free, caffeine- and alcohol-free mornings.
locator: Abstract; Methods; Results; Table 1; Figures 1-2; Discussion (tablet accuracy +/-0.25 mm; physiologic tremor not measurable)
limitations: n=18 trial volunteers; spirals, not writing; averaging over hands; distribution fraction estimates are this ledger's lognormal derivation (95% CI of GM ~0.10-0.42 cm gives <=1 mm fraction ~17-51%); tablet floor +/-0.25 mm makes fractions below ~0.5 mm unreliable; practice effect from day 1 to 2.
relevance_to_design: The only retrieved per-patient amplitude distribution in mm. Median ET spiral tremor (~2 mm p-p) is about twice what +/-0.5 mm per axis can fully cancel. FTM 1 ('slight') already implies ~2 mm p-p.
transferability_reason: Peak-to-peak mm directly comparable to nib stroke, but spirals, not handwriting, and a small trial population off medication.
design_implication: Best estimate: about one third (plausible 15-50%) of trial-type ET patients have tremor <=1 mm p-p, which is fully within +/-0.5 mm. Above 2 mm p-p, an ideal single-axis clip gives <=50% reduction, below the 51% tablet MDC. Replicate with handwriting and sub-0.1 mm instrumentation.

topic: ET writing tremor on a digitising tablet
citation: Elble RJ, Brilliant M, Leffler K, Higgins C. Quantification of essential tremor in writing and drawing. Mov Disord 1996;11(1):70-78.
task_or_setup: Two series of cursive e's and l's on ruled paper on a commercial digitising tablet; 40 also drew an Archimedes spiral; postural wrist tremor by triaxial accelerometer.
key_quantitative_findings: Tablet sensitive enough to measure sustained visible tremor; very severe tremor could not be recorded when the pen could not stay on the tablet. Intertrial variability: a 36.0% change in mean writing acceleration amplitude and 8.3% change in frequency detectable in 30 patients (p=0.01, power 90%); accelerometry 35.9% and 7.8%. Wrist vs writing tremor correlation <0.60 for amplitude and <0.25 for frequency. Age-frequency and amplitude-frequency correlations existed for posture but not for writing or drawing.
units_and_conditions: Acceleration amplitude (cm/s^2) and Hz; displacement not given in abstract.
locator: Abstract
limitations: Abstract only; no mm displacement or frequency ranges available; clinic ET sample.
relevance_to_design: Writing tremor differs from postural tremor and cannot be inferred from wrist or posture measurements.
transferability_reason: Writing-specific and large n, but acceleration units only.
design_implication: Size the actuator and the correction algorithm from writing-task data, not from postural or spiral data alone.
search_query: Europe PMC REST: DOI:"10.1002/mds.870110113"

topic: TETRAS: item anchors (cm) and reliability; spiral and handwriting items
citation: Elble R, Comella C, Fahn S, Hallett M, Jankovic J, Juncos JL, Lewitt P, Lyons K, Ondo W, Pahwa R, Sethi K, Stover N, Tarsy D, Testa C, Tintner R, Watts R, Zesiewicz T. Reliability of a new scale for essential tremor. Mov Disord 2012;27(12):1567-1569.
task_or_setup: Videos rated by 10 specialists twice, 1-2 months apart, with TETRAS: 9 performance items rated 0-4 in half points. Head and limb items defined by amplitude ranges in cm.
participants_or_bench: Videos of 44 ET patients and 6 controls
key_quantitative_findings: Upper-limb anchors (Table 1): 1 = barely visible; 1.5 = <1 cm; 2 = 1 to <3 cm; 2.5 = 3 to <5 cm; 3 = 5 to <10 cm; 3.5 = 10 to <20 cm; 4 = >20 cm. Inter-/intra-rater ICC 0.86-0.96 for head and upper-limb items; total score ICC 0.94 and 0.96. Spiral and handwriting item wording (as quoted by Ondo et al. 2021, doi:10.5334/tohm.665): spiral 0 none, 1 slight 'barely visible', 2 mild 'obvious', 3 moderate 'portions not recognizable', 4 severe 'figure not recognizable'; handwriting 0 none, 1 slight 'untidy', 2 mild 'legible but considerable tremor', 3 moderate 'parts illegible', 4 severe 'completely illegible'.
units_and_conditions: cm ranges for limb items (the peak vs peak-to-peak convention was not confirmed in retrieved text); spiral and handwriting items have no cm anchors.
locator: Abstract; Table 1; (spiral/handwriting wording: Ondo et al. 2021, tohm.665, Introduction)
limitations: Spiral and handwriting items are defined only by visual or legibility descriptors. Ondo et al. 2021 found rater agreement 'good for spirals but poor for handwriting samples'.
relevance_to_design: Even TETRAS grade 1.5 limb tremor is up to 1 cm, and writing items lack metric anchors.
transferability_reason: Standard ET trial instrument.
design_implication: Use TETRAS handwriting and spiral items as secondary outcomes only, with quantitative nib or tablet displacement in mm as the primary engineering outcome.

topic: Physiological hand tremor: displacement amplitude and frequency
citation: Stiles RN. Frequency and displacement amplitude relations for normal hand tremor. J Appl Physiol 1976;40(1):44-54.
task_or_setup: Spectral analysis of hand tremor during continuous hand extension for 15-45 min, with extensor EMG.
participants_or_bench: Normal subjects (number not in abstract)
key_quantitative_findings: Control RMS displacement ~30 um at 8-9 Hz. With prolonged extension, RMS displacement rose to 'on the order of 100-1,000 times control' and frequency fell to 4-6 Hz. Below ~100 um RMS a viscoelastic-mass mechanism dominated. A 30 um RMS sinusoid is ~85 um peak-to-peak (derived).
units_and_conditions: um RMS displacement; outstretched hand posture, not writing.
locator: Abstract
limitations: Abstract only; posture not writing; fatiguing protocol for the large values; small historic sample.
relevance_to_design: Normal physiological tremor (~0.03 mm RMS) sits far inside +/-0.5 mm and below tablet accuracy (+/-0.25 mm). It is not visible in writing unless enhanced.
transferability_reason: Hand posture rather than pen tip in writing.
design_implication: For non-clinical users, cancelling physiological tremor is within stroke range but probably gives no visible writing benefit. Verify perceptibility before claiming any benefit.

topic: PD intervention: intensive amplitude (writing-size) training RCT
citation: Nackaerts E, Heremans E, Vervoort G, Smits-Engelsman BC, Swinnen SP, Vandenberghe W, Bergmans B, Nieuwboer A. Relearning of Writing Skills in Parkinson's Disease After Intensive Amplitude Training. Mov Disord 2016;31(8):1209-1216.
task_or_setup: Placebo-controlled RCT. Amplitude training (pen-and-paper and touch-sensitive tablet exercises with visual cues) vs stretch/relaxation, both 30 min/day, 5 days/week, 6 weeks. Assessed pre, post and after 6-week retention on a tablet (200 Hz, 32.5 um resolution per companion paper) and a pen-and-paper test (SOS).
participants_or_bench: 38 right-handed PD (H&Y I-III, ON; MDS-UPDRS 2.7 >=1); experimental n=18, placebo n=20
key_quantitative_findings: Training improved writing amplitude and amplitude variability on transfer tasks (trained and untrained sequences, with and without target zones) and automatization tasks (single and dual task). Effect sizes 7-17%, maintained after 6-week retention, with transfer to daily-life writing.
units_and_conditions: Writing amplitude change (%) on tablet; ON medication.
locator: Abstract; training details from companion PLoS One 2017 (PDT-17) Methods
limitations: Abstract only for this paper; early-mid PD; modest gains; see PDT-17 for fluency costs.
relevance_to_design: Best RCT evidence that PD writing size can be relearned with 15 h of cued practice, with retention and transfer.
transferability_reason: RCT with placebo, retention and transfer tests; tablet and visual-cue training is replicable in a pen plus app.
design_implication: Guided-practice mode should copy the dose (30 min x 5/week x 6 weeks), target zones and progression. Monitor fluency alongside size.

topic: PD intervention trade-off: size vs speed vs fluency
citation: Nackaerts E, Broeder S, Pereira MP, Swinnen SP, Vandenberghe W, Nieuwboer A, Heremans E. Handwriting training in Parkinson's disease: A trade-off between size, speed and fluency. PLoS One 2017;12(12):e0190223.
task_or_setup: Same RCT as PDT-16. Touch-sensitive tablet (200 Hz; 32.5 um) pre, post and at 6-week retention. Outcomes: stroke duration (s), velocity (cm/s), normalized jerk (unit-free), built from (1/2) x integral of j(t)^2 dt x duration^5 / length^2, where j(t) is the third time derivative of position. Whether a square root is applied could not be checked from the HTML rendering.
participants_or_bench: 38 right-handed PD (H&Y I-III; ON); experimental 18, placebo 20
key_quantitative_findings: After amplitude training, stroke duration and normalized jerk increased (less fluent), e.g. automatization large-amplitude: duration group x time F=11.434, p<0.001; jerk F=8.928, p<0.001; transfer: duration F=18.237, p<0.001; jerk F=8.732, p<0.001. Velocity unchanged in the training group; the placebo group increased velocity. Increases persisted at retention. Larger jerk increase correlated with lower MMSE (r=-0.734 post; r=-0.676 retention).
units_and_conditions: s, cm/s, normalized jerk; ON medication.
locator: Abstract; Methods (outcomes, jerk formula); Results; Figure 2; Figure 4
limitations: No EMG or mechanism data; secondary outcomes of a modest RCT; cognition link based on correlations.
relevance_to_design: Bigger writing came at the cost of slower, less fluent strokes.
transferability_reason: Same RCT with robust tablet kinematics.
design_implication: Any size cue or feedback mode must report fluency (jerk or velocity peaks) and duration, not just size. Avoid rewarding size alone. Take care with cognitively impaired users.

topic: PD cueing: visual target-line spacing (0.6 vs 1.0 cm)
citation: Nackaerts E, Nieuwboer A, Broeder S, Smits-Engelsman BC, Swinnen SP, Vandenberghe W, Heremans E. Opposite Effects of Visual Cueing During Writing-Like Movements of Different Amplitudes in Parkinson's Disease. Neurorehabil Neural Repair 2016;30(5):431-439.
task_or_setup: Prewriting loop task at 0.6 cm and 1.0 cm, with and without visual target lines, on a touch-sensitive tablet.
participants_or_bench: 15 PD; 15 age-matched healthy controls
key_quantitative_findings: At 1.0 cm, cues immediately improved writing size, size variability and speed in both groups. At 0.6 cm, cues decreased writing size in both groups (P<.001), the cued-uncued variability difference disappeared, and controls slowed with cues.
units_and_conditions: Writing amplitude (cm), variability, speed; immediate effects only.
locator: Abstract
limitations: Abstract only; immediate effects; prewriting loops, not text.
relevance_to_design: The spacing of a visual cue matters: narrow cues (0.6 cm) act as accuracy constraints and shrink writing.
transferability_reason: Loop task; immediate effect; small n.
design_implication: Any on-paper or projected guide should be at least ~1.0 cm. Avoid narrow guides in PD modes.

topic: PD cueing: visual dots and verbal 'big' reminders
citation: Oliveira RM, Gurd JM, Nixon P, Marshall JC, Passingham RE. Micrographia in Parkinson's disease: the effect of providing external cues. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1997;63(4):429-433.
task_or_setup: Stylus on a graphics tablet. Free writing; writing with dots marking the required size; writing with continuous verbal reminders ('big'). Each condition done twice.
participants_or_bench: 11 PD (mean age 65.4 y); 14 controls (67.1 y)
key_quantitative_findings: Amplitude became more normal with visual cues and with auditory (verbal) reminders. Improvement persisted in free writing shortly afterwards. Amplitude increased mainly through longer movement time, not higher peak velocity.
units_and_conditions: Amplitude and kinematics on tablet; exact values not in abstract (scanned full text not retrievable).
locator: Abstract (PMC2169751)
limitations: Abstract only; n=11; short-term only; no mm values extracted.
relevance_to_design: Both visual and attentional/verbal cues enlarge PD writing, but by slowing it.
transferability_reason: Small lab study; consistent with later work (PDT-16 to PDT-18).
design_implication: Cueing modes can be visual, haptic or audio prompts to 'write big', but should monitor the speed cost.

topic: PD lined-paper practice RCT: diverging vs parallel lines (home, self-managed)
citation: Andreoli D, Reed A, Coe S, Dawes H, Collett J. An Exploratory Randomised Trial of a Self-Managed Home-Based Exaggerated Spatial Cueing Intervention for Handwriting in Parkinson's Disease. Disabilities 2025;5(4):93.
task_or_setup: Assessor-blind two-arm RCT (NCT03369587). 6-week, 5x/week daily diary on lined paper: diverging lines (10 mm increasing to 13 mm apart) vs parallel lines (10 mm).
participants_or_bench: 48 people with PD and self-reported handwriting problems (24 per arm; 19 and 20 analysed)
key_quantitative_findings: Median diary entries 31 (IQR 17.5-39) vs 30 requested; no group difference (p=0.302). No adverse events. Regardless of group: 'el' speed d=-0.90 (single task, p=0.001) and d=-0.72 (dual task); 'el' amplitude d=1.07 (single, p<0.001) and 0.86 (dual, p=0.002); sentence amplitude d=0.80 (p=0.003); perceived difficulty improved (OR -3.6, p=0.047). Between-group effects small (d=0.11-0.48).
units_and_conditions: Cohen's d; home practice; medication state not stated in abstract.
locator: Abstract (Crossref record); CC BY 4.0
limitations: Abstract only (publisher page returned 403); exploratory; no untreated control arm, so practice and cueing effects are confounded; dropout ~19%.
relevance_to_design: Low-resource, well-adhered home practice gave large within-group gains in size and speed. Exaggerated (diverging) cues added little.
transferability_reason: Randomised, blinded assessor, home setting similar to intended use.
design_implication: A practice mode built on daily writing with simple spatial guides is supported. Fancy cue geometry is not. Include a no-practice control in our own trials.

topic: PD: weighted pen and auditory cues (metronome, music)
citation: Latimer N, Reelfs A, Halbert J, Hansen J, Miller A, Barton C, Stuhr J, Zaman A, Stegemöller EL. The effects of auditory cues and weighted pens on handwriting in individuals with Parkinson's disease. J Hand Ther 2024;37(1):144-152.
task_or_setup: Continuous cursive 'l's on 1.5-cm-lined paper for 10 s with a standard vs weighted pen, under 4 auditory conditions (silence, metronome, activating music, relaxing music). Pen-tip kinematic sensors; EMG of extensor digitorum communis (EDC) and first dorsal interosseous.
participants_or_bench: 8 older adults with PD (pilot cohort)
key_quantitative_findings: Standard pen, peak-to-peak time: control 0.807 +/- 0.121 s vs metronome 0.701 +/- 0.100 s (p=0.024) and activating music 0.691 +/- 0.113 s (p=0.009). Weighted vs standard pen: variability of distance between letter peaks 0.482 +/- 0.065 vs 0.187 +/- 0.010 (p=0.033); variability of letter time 0.187 +/- 0.016 vs 0.176 +/- 0.010 (p=0.042). EDC EMG area reduced with metronome (66.03 vs 88.98 mV) and activating music (66.49 vs 88.98 mV).
units_and_conditions: s; variability indices; mV (EMG AUC); single session; pen mass not stated in abstract.
locator: Abstract
limitations: n=8; single session; novice weighted-pen users; weighted-pen mass not available; no tremor measure.
relevance_to_design: Only pen-specific mass evidence in PD: added mass increased spatial and temporal variability. Rhythmic auditory cues sped writing and reduced extensor activity.
transferability_reason: Direct pen study but tiny pilot.
design_implication: Do not add mass for PD users without testing; keep the pen's total mass and inertia close to normal pens. An auditory rhythm cue mode is worth piloting.

topic: ET: inertial (mass) loading and postural tremor
citation: Héroux ME, Pari G, Norman KE. The effect of inertial loading on wrist postural tremor in essential tremor. Clin Neurophysiol 2009;120(5):1020-1029.
task_or_setup: Outstretched hand supporting submaximal loads (none, 5%, 15%, 25% of 1-repetition maximum); hand postural tremor and wrist extensor EMG.
participants_or_bench: 23 ET; 22 controls
key_quantitative_findings: Inertial loading reduced postural tremor in all ET subjects. The largest reduction occurred between 5% and 15% loads, associated with spectral separation of mechanical-reflex and central components. EMG tremor power did not increase with loading.
units_and_conditions: Postural wrist tremor; loads defined as % of 1-RM (absolute masses not in abstract); not writing.
locator: Abstract
limitations: Abstract only; postural task; loads likely much larger than feasible pen-mass changes; no functional or writing outcome.
relevance_to_design: Mechanism for why added mass can reduce ET tremor. Transfer to a pen of a few tens of grams is unknown.
transferability_reason: Posture with heavy loads; not a pen or writing.
design_implication: Do not assume a heavier pen helps ET writing. If mass is used, test it on writing-tremor displacement with the actuator on and off.

topic: Active cancellation handheld device (Liftware/ACT spoon) in ET
citation: Pathak A, Redmond JA, Allen M, Chou KL. A noninvasive handheld assistive device to accommodate essential tremor: a pilot study. Mov Disord 2014;29(6):838-842.
task_or_setup: Holding, eating and transferring tasks with the active-cancellation-of-tremor (ACT) spoon on vs off. FTM TRS ratings; CGI-S; embedded accelerometer amplitude by double integration at the dominant frequency.
participants_or_bench: 15 ET (9 M, 6 F; TRS total 47.9 +/- 14.3; feeding item 2.6 +/- 0.9); accelerometer data analysable in 11. Device ~100 g, 40 x 50 x 175 mm.
key_quantitative_findings: Change in TRS item from baseline (improvement) with device on vs off, blinded on/off tests: holding 1.00 +/- 0.76 vs 0.27 +/- 0.70 (P=0.016); eating 1.47 +/- 1.06 vs 0.13 +/- 0.64 (P=0.001); transferring 1.33 +/- 0.82 vs 0.27 +/- 0.59 (P=0.001). Accelerometer tremor reduction 71-76% (holding 72%, eating 76%, transferring 71%). Two subjects with severe tremor (DBS off) could not use the device.
units_and_conditions: Rating points; % reduction of accelerometer-derived amplitude; actuator stroke not reported.
locator: Abstract; Methods (device description; TRS change calculation); Table 2; Results; Discussion (PMC4156033)
limitations: Pilot, n=15 (11 with accelerometer data); feeding tasks, not writing; actuator stroke and bandwidth not reported; short-term use only.
relevance_to_design: Closest human evidence that handheld active cancellation reduces ET task tremor, but with a spoon-sized actuator, ~100 g device and a range limit that excluded severe tremor.
transferability_reason: Same principle, different task, stroke and mass.
design_implication: Define and publish the pen's stroke limit and expected exclusion of larger tremor up front. Use on-vs-off crossover designs with blinded raters.

topic: Liftware Steady and weighted/built-up/swivel spoons in PD- and ET-related tremor
citation: Sabari J, Stefanov DG, Chan J, Goed L, Starr J. Adapted Feeding Utensils for People With Parkinson's-Related or Essential Tremor. Am J Occup Ther 2019;73(2):7302205120p1-7302205120p9.
task_or_setup: Simulated feeding under 5 conditions: standard spoon; weighted spoon (standard handle); weighted spoon (built-up handle); swivel spoon; Liftware Steady (active cancellation). Participants rated each against the standard spoon.
participants_or_bench: People with ET or PD-related tremor (n not stated in abstract)
key_quantitative_findings: Participants preferred Liftware Steady and the weighted spoon with standard handle. Friedman's test found no significant difference in ratings between these two. Reactions and reasons varied.
units_and_conditions: Subjective ratings (performance, ease, speed, neatness, aesthetics).
locator: Abstract
limitations: Abstract only; subjective outcomes; feeding task; PD and ET results not separated in abstract.
relevance_to_design: In PD/ET users, a passive weighted utensil was rated about as well as an active-cancellation device.
transferability_reason: Feeding, subjective; no writing.
design_implication: Benchmark the active pen against passive alternatives (standard pen, a weighted/wide-grip pen) in user trials. Let users trial before purchase.

topic: Smart pen prototype for tremor mitigation (adaptive filtering)
citation: Tironi JC, Fernandes A, Borges RC, Silva LA, Parreira WD. A smart pen prototype with adaptive algorithms for stabilizing handwriting tremor signals in Parkinson's disease. Sci Rep 2025;15(1):28659.
task_or_setup: ADXL345 accelerometer, Teensy 4.1 microcontroller and 3 V coin vibration motor (up to 9000 rpm). Fx-LMS, Fx-NLMS, combined, RLS and Kalman algorithms simulated on NewHandPD signals from 31 PD patients, then tested on the microcontroller and an orbital shaking table (constant and variable speed).
participants_or_bench: No human participants; signals from the NewHandPD dataset; shaking table
key_quantitative_findings: Simulation MSE: Fx-LMS -38 dB (~600 iterations to converge), Fx-NLMS -42 dB (~400), combined -44 dB (~350), RLS -53 dB (~300), Kalman -50 dB (~50). Kalman converged ~8x faster than RLS. Shaking table: ~-37 dB MSE after 60 iterations (constant speed); ~-26 dB (variable speed). No % tremor attenuation at the pen tip and no handwriting outcome reported.
units_and_conditions: dB MSE of signal estimation; iterations; lab only.
locator: Proposed solution; Results; Table 1; Figures 4-6; Conclusion
limitations: No users; a vibration motor cannot impose controlled nib displacement; tremor amplitude and frequency and shaking-table settings not reported. The paper describes NewHandPD with HandPD's figures (736 images, 92 individuals) and says the motion data were 'recorded at 200 Hz', whereas NewHandPD file headers state 1000 Hz (PDT-29).
relevance_to_design: Algorithmic precedent only. No evidence that a pen improves PD handwriting.
transferability_reason: Simulation and bench; different actuation principle.
design_implication: Do not cite as clinical evidence. Kalman-type estimators' fast convergence is worth benchmarking, but any claim needs human writing trials measuring nib displacement.
search_query: Europe PMC REST: DOI:"10.1038/s41598-025-14196-5"; WebFetch: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12325923/

topic: SteadyScrib pen and clipboard (magnetic, weighted, wide grip)
citation: SteadyScrib. The SteadyScrib Parkinson's Pen Set (product page); Northwestern Now, 'A pen designed for Parkinson's patients', 6 March 2023.

topic: Outcome measure: SOS-test (Systematic Screening of Handwriting Difficulties) in PD
citation: Nackaerts E, Heremans E, Smits-Engelsman BC, Broeder S, Vandenberghe W, Bergmans B, Nieuwboer A. Validity and reliability of a new tool to evaluate handwriting difficulties in Parkinson's disease. PLoS One 2017;12(3):e0173157.
task_or_setup: Copy text for 5 minutes with a normal pen. First five lines scored 0-2 on each of 5 criteria (fluency of letter formation, connections between letters, regularity of letter size, space between words, straightness of sentence; total 0-10, higher = worse). Speed = letters in 5 min. Writing size also measured.
participants_or_bench: 87 PD (67 retested); 26 healthy controls
key_quantitative_findings: Inter-rater ICC: speed 0.999, score 0.769; size rho 0.860. Test-retest ICC: speed 0.965, score 0.806; size rho 0.807. SEM/MDC: score 0.800/2.218 points; speed 22.374/62.018 letters. PD vs controls: higher SOS score (p=0.031), smaller size (p=0.043), slower speed (p<0.001). Correlations: speed with Purdue pegboard (rho=0.420) and MDS-UPDRS-III (rho=-0.376).
units_and_conditions: SOS points (0-10); letters per 5 min; ON medication.
locator: Methods; Table 2 (validity); Table 3 (reliability, SEM, MDC); Results
limitations: No MCID or cut-offs; Dutch-language text; score sensitive to rater training.
relevance_to_design: A validated paper-and-pen legibility and speed outcome that works without instrumentation. The MDC of ~2.2 points sets a detectable-change bar.
transferability_reason: Validated in PD and used in RCTs (PDT-16) and remote programmes.
design_implication: Use SOS score and speed as participant-level functional outcomes in pen trials alongside nib or tablet kinematics. Power studies against MDC 2.2 points.
